127.title: Your simran
127.hook: settle on a time and a length that fits your life
127.howItsDone: Sikhs keep simran in many ways: alone before dawn, in short moments through the day, or together in the gurdwara where the sangat repeats Waheguru in rhythm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simran under the work: Namdev at his dyes, hands and feet busy, heart with the One. Your line was hands at work, heart at home.
screen: `SIMRAN — HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Every January, someone at the gym promises themselves an hour a day, every day, forever. By February, the plan is gone. Not from laziness: the plan never fit their actual life. Prayer and meditation can go the same way. It's easy to picture the ideal version, the saint up at three, sitting still for hours, and to count anything less as failure. This is the last day of this stretch on simran, and it isn't a new technique. It's a plan that fits you.
screen: `AN HOUR A DAY, FOREVER.` → `GONE BY FEBRUARY.` → `A PLAN THAT FITS YOUR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week's tools. Waheguru on the breath, Wahe in, Guru out. Satnam: true name. Coming back when the mind runs off. The early hour, amrit vela. The mala, bead by bead. And the Name running under your work. None of these are rules you must follow. They're tools, and Sikhs use them in many combinations. Some do simran for an hour before dawn. Some do five minutes on the bus. Some join the sangat for simran at the gurdwara, the whole room repeating Waheguru in rhythm. The Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to rise early and meditate on the Name, and many take that as a daily anchor, but the Gurus never set a minimum number of minutes. What the Guru Granth Sahib keeps returning to is remembering, done again and again, not once in a heroic burst. So, three questions. When? A time that already exists in your day: waking up, a coffee, a commute, before sleep. Where? A real place: the edge of the bed, a chair, the car before you go in. How long? Smaller than you think. Five minutes, done every day, beats an hour done once. And if a day gets missed, simran already has its answer. You just come back.

segments.voice: Walk through tomorrow in your mind, from waking up, and find a gap: before you check your phone, right after you drop the kids, when you park the car. Picture yourself there doing five minutes of whichever simran you liked best this week, or, if you're here to learn, five minutes of quiet breathing. Stay in that picture a while.
Your simran. Remembering the Name, at a time, a place and a length that fit your real life, done steadily.
Your line: your five minutes. Small, steady, and yours to come back to. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: The daily banis
128.hook: Nitnem means daily practice: set prayers at dawn, at dusk and at night
128.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Nitnem daily: Japji, Jaap and the Savaiyas (and often Chaupai and Anand) in the morning, Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, from memory, from a gutka or along with a recording.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your simran: a time, a place and a length that fit your real life. Your line was your five minutes. And if a day slips, there's always coming back.

A daily routine can run almost unnoticed. Coffee before anything. The same podcast on the drive. Checking the locks at night. Small repeated things hold a day together, like the hinges on a door. Sikhs have a routine like this too, but it's made of words. At dawn, at dusk and at night, many Sikhs recite set hymns from the Gurus. Not new words each day. The same words, day after day, for years, until they're part of the person.
screen: `COFFEE, PODCAST, LOCKS.` → `A ROUTINE MADE OF WORDS.` → `DAWN, DUSK AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The routine is called Nitnem. Nit means daily, always. Nem means a rule, a discipline, a vow you keep. So Nitnem is the daily discipline: a set of banis, hymns from the Gurus, said at fixed times. Bani simply means the word, the Guru's utterance. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, lays out three times. Morning: Japji Sahib, by Guru Nanak, then Jaap Sahib and the ten Savaiyas, by Guru Gobind Singh. Many Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five banis in the morning, adding Chaupai Sahib and Anand Sahib. Evening, at sunset: Rehras Sahib. Night, before sleep: Kirtan Sohila, which you met on day one hundred thirteen. Three doors in the day, each opened with the Guru's words. Some Sikh traditions and jathas include a few more banis or slightly longer versions; that comes later. Why the same words every day? Walk across a field once and it's just grass. Walk it every day and it becomes a path, and your feet find it in the dark. Daily banis can work like that on the mind. Over years, the lines surface on their own: in traffic, at a hospital bed, at a wedding. And Nitnem isn't only for the devout few. Children learn it at home, grandparents keep it, and many Sikhs listen along to a recording on the way to work. In the coming days, each bani gets its own day, plainly, one at a time.

129.title: Japji at dawn
129.hook: Guru Nanak's Japji is the first morning bani
129.howItsDone: Japji Sahib is the first bani of the Sikh morning; many Sikhs recite it from memory or from a gutka in the amrit vela, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nitnem: set banis at dawn, at dusk and at night. Your line was morning, evening, night. Today, the first door opens.

Before sunrise in Sikh homes around the world, from Amritsar to Toronto to Nairobi, the same words are being said. A grandfather in a kitchen, murmuring from memory. A student with a small prayer book on her knee. A taxi driver with a recording playing low. For those who say it, it's the first thing the day hears. And it's the same hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself. Page one.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, EVERYWHERE.` → `THE FIRST THING THE DAY HEARS.` → `PAGE ONE OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Japji Sahib is by Guru Nanak. Jap means to recite, to repeat, to meditate on; ji and sahib are words of respect. So it's the honored recitation. It begins with the Mul Mantar, the root verse you know: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one God, whose name is truth. Then a short salok: God was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true. Then thirty-eight pauris, stanzas, and a closing salok. The first pauri is a surprise. Before telling you how to find God, Guru Nanak tells you what doesn't work. In paraphrase: thinking won't do it, even a hundred thousand times. Silence won't do it, even if you sit silent forever. Piling up the world's goods won't satisfy hunger. Thousands upon thousands of clever tricks, and not one goes with you. So how? The stanza closes with the answer: by walking in the hukam, the Divine Order, the Will, which is written with us. From there, Japji travels through the whole of life: listening, trusting, the vastness of creation, and at the end five realms of the spirit, rising to the realm of truth. The last salok, in paraphrase, calls air the guru, water the father, the great earth the mother, and day and night the two nurses in whose laps the whole world plays. One unusual detail: nearly every hymn in the Granth is set to a raag, a musical mode, for singing. Japji isn't. It's meant to be recited: plain spoken words at the start of the day.

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of Japji Sahib and listen to the first minute or two, the Mul Mantar and the start of the first pauri; you don't need to understand the Punjabi. Let the sound be the first thing in this moment, the way it is for many Sikhs at dawn. If you can't play it, sit quietly and hear in your mind the two words you already know: Ik Onkar.

130.title: Jaap Sahib
130.hook: Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in quick changing meters
130.howItsDone: Jaap Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, is the second bani of the Sikh morning Nitnem and is also recited during the Amrit ceremony; many Sikhs know its quick rhythms by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji Sahib: page one of the Granth, recited plain at dawn. Your line was begin with japji. Today, the bani that comes right after it.

Some music makes it impossible to sit still. A drumline at a parade. A song where the beat suddenly doubles and the whole crowd jumps. Japji is calm, like a teacher talking. The next bani in the Sikh morning is something else. It gallops. The lines are short, the rhythm keeps changing, and when a whole room recites it together it can feel like running downhill. It was written by the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh.
screen: `A DRUMLINE, A DOUBLED BEAT.` → `JAPJI IS CALM.` → `THE NEXT ONE GALLOPS.`

segments.voice: Jaap Sahib is a long hymn of praise, about two hundred short verses. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. It's in a separate collection called the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth Guru, and it's said every morning in Nitnem and at the Amrit ceremony, when Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa. It praises Akal, the Timeless One, and much of it describes God by what God is not. The opening, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage; whose form and shape and garb no one can describe. Then it rolls into salutations, line after line, each beginning with a word of bowing: salutation to the Timeless, to the Merciful, to the One without form, to the One without a name. Hundreds of names, most of them saying: beyond this, beyond that. The words keep reaching, and keep admitting they can't reach. Then there's the rhythm. Guru Gobind Singh was a poet as well as a leader, and he wrote Jaap in many different meters, chhands, switching from one to another as the hymn goes on. Some sections are slow and stately. Some are so quick the syllables tumble. The language mixes Braj, Sanskrit, Punjabi and even Persian and Arabic words, as if praise needed every language he knew. You don't have to follow the meaning to feel what it's doing. It's praise with a heartbeat, and the heartbeat keeps changing.

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of Jaap Sahib and listen for the rhythm rather than every word: where it speeds up, where it slows down, tapping the beat lightly on your knee if that helps. If you can't play anything, sit and breathe, and notice your own rhythm, your heartbeat and your breath, praising without words.

131.title: Tav Prasad Savaiye
131.hook: ten verses saying that kings, armies and rituals are nothing without love
131.howItsDone: The ten Tav Prasad Savaiye, from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, are recited every morning in Nitnem after Jaap Sahib, and are among the five banis of the Amrit ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaap Sahib: Guru Gobind Singh's galloping praise, beyond every name. Your line was the rhythm of praise. Today, the same Guru, in a very different mood.

Scroll any feed for five minutes and you'll see what the world calls impressive. The mansion. The supercar. The influencer at a holy site at sunrise, perfectly lit. Followers in the millions. Centuries ago a poet saw the equivalent of all that in his own day, the richest kings, the biggest armies, the most admired ascetics and pilgrims, and he wrote ten short poems that keep turning back to one thought. All of it, he says, is worth nothing, without one thing.
screen: `THE MANSION, THE SUPERCAR.` → `THE PERFECT HOLY PHOTO.` → `ALL OF IT, WORTH NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The poems are the Tav Prasad Savaiye, the third bani of the Sikh morning. Tav prasad means by your grace. Savaiya is the poetic form: a four-line verse with long, flowing lines, beautiful to recite. These ten come from Guru Gobind Singh's Akal Ustat, the praise of the Timeless, in the Dasam Granth. Each verse is a parade. In paraphrase: I have seen the pure ascetics, the yogis, the celibates, crowds of them. I have seen mighty kings riding elephants with golden trappings, great horses, armies without number, emperors who conquered the earth. I have seen pilgrims bathing at every holy river, people fasting, people performing every ritual. Then, as the verses close, the turn: without the Lord, without love, none of it counts for anything. And the famous line, again in paraphrase: I tell the truth, listen, everyone: only those who loved found the Lord. Notice who is saying this. Guru Gobind Singh was himself a leader of armies, who knew horses and weapons and power from the inside. He's not sneering at kings from the outside. From someone who knew that world, the savaiyas say: it isn't the thing. Neither, they say, is outward religion done without love. They're gentle with no one's pride, including the pride of the pious. What remains after the parade passes? Love. That's why these ten verses sit in the morning. Before the day starts measuring you by what you own or how you look, the savaiyas measure differently.

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of Tav Prasad Savaiye and listen to just the first verse, about a minute, noticing the long, rolling lines. If you can't, hold one thing you've been proud of lately, a promotion, a purchase, a good photo, and ask the savaiyas' question: was there love in it? No judgment, just the question.

132.title: Chaupai Sahib
132.hook: a prayer asking to be kept under the Guru's protecting hand
132.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib as part of the morning banis and within Rehras in the evening, and some say it at times of fear, before travel or at a hospital bedside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the savaiyas: kings, armies and rituals paraded past, and only those who loved found the Lord. Your line was without love, nothing.

A child is crossing a busy road. Halfway across, without looking up, the small hand reaches out, and a bigger hand closes around it. Nobody has to say anything. Grown-ups have their own versions of that moment: a diagnosis, a turbulent flight, a phone call at two in the morning. Sikhs have a prayer built around that reach. Some say it every day, and some say it again when they're afraid.
screen: `A SMALL HAND REACHES OUT.` → `TURBULENCE, A 2 A.M. CALL.` → `A PRAYER FOR THE REACH.`

segments.voice: It's called Chaupai Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, from the Dasam Granth. Its full name is often given as Benti Chaupai: benti means a humble request, and chaupai is the verse form, short lines grouped in fours. Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite it in the morning, it's part of the evening Rehras, and it's one of the banis read at the Amrit ceremony. The whole of it is one long request: keep me. The opening, in paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Let my mind stay at your feet; cherish me as your own. Then the prayer widens. It asks to be kept from enemies, from harm, from those who would do wrong. It praises the One who creates and sustains everything, who knows each heart from inside. And it keeps returning to that picture of the hand. What's striking is that it's a request at all. Its author was the tenth Guru, and Sikh tradition remembers the hardships of his life: his father's execution, and later the deaths of his sons. Yet the prayer has no swagger in it. It speaks as someone asking to be carried. Some people expect a prayer for protection to promise that nothing bad will happen. Chaupai doesn't promise that; the Guru's own life didn't look like that. It asks to be held, to be counted as one of God's own, whatever comes. That's the reach the child makes on the road. Not a guarantee. A hand.

133.hook: Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, part of the morning or evening prayers
133.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning; its short form of six pauris is sung near the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, before Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai Sahib, the prayer for a hand. Your line was keep me. This week: your simran, Nitnem, Japji Sahib, Jaap's gallop, the savaiyas, Chaupai. Today the morning set is complete.
screen: `YOUR SIMRAN · NITNEM · JAPJI · JAAP · SAVAIYAS · CHAUPAI.`

segments.voice: A wedding. A child's naming. A memorial. An ordinary Sunday service. Four very different mornings in a gurdwara, and near the end of each one, the same short song. The Sikh code of conduct asks for it at the close of services, so it's sung over happy occasions and sad ones alike, and then everyone stands for the prayer called Ardas. It's the song of bliss, written by the third Guru.
screen: `A WEDDING, A NAMING, A MEMORIAL.` → `THE SAME SONG NEAR THE END.` → `THE SONG OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Anand means bliss, deep joy. Anand Sahib is by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and it's in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raag Ramkali: forty pauris. Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty in the morning, after Chaupai. A shorter form, the first five pauris and the last, is sung at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and part of it is said in the evening Rehras too. The first line is where the whole song lives. In paraphrase: joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. Notice who the line is spoken to. Not a crowd. O my mother. It sounds like someone bursting through the kitchen door with news. And notice the tense. Joy has come. Not a wish: something that happened. The line goes on to say the Guru was found with sahaj, with ease, naturally, and that the heart is filled with music. Then the pauris turn the joy over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. What is real joy? Everyone talks about bliss, the song says, but bliss is known through the Guru. True anand comes from the Name and the Guru's word, and the song asks the listener to sing that word. So this bliss isn't the same as having no troubles. That's how it can be sung at funerals as well as weddings: the joy sits underneath, a sense of having been found. Tradition says Guru Amar Das found his Guru late, when he was already in his sixties. Joy, found, even then.
screen: `ANAND — BLISS, DEEP JOY.` · `JOY HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.` · `FOUND WITH EASE, SAHAJ.` · `AT WEDDINGS AND AT FUNERALS.` · then, large: `JOY, FOUND.`

segments.voice: If you can, play about a minute of Anand Sahib's first pauri and let the opening line land: joy has come, O my mother. If not, remember a moment you ran to tell someone good news: who you told, and how it felt to say it out loud. Sit inside that moment, then let it settle into something quieter.
